name: lemmeknow
why: Identifies unknown strings and ciphers by pattern, a fun way to examine mystery data, though a narrow tool.

brief.what_it_is: lemmeknow is a command-line tool, written in Rust, that tries to identify what a piece of mysterious text is. You give it a string or a filename as the argument, and it reports what the input looks like. The README says it can analyze hard-coded strings from captured network packets, malware, or just about anything. The README does not show the output format in text; a screenshot demo is embedded and a `--json` flag switches output to JSON. There is also a web version at swanandx.github.io/lemmeknow-frontend and a Rust crate for use in other projects.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it exists to identify mysterious text quickly, and it calls itself 'The fastest way to identify anything.' It is inspired by PyWhat, a Python tool with the same goal, and the README credits PyWhat's developer for the idea.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the mechanism in detail. Its contributing section says people can add or improve regex patterns and improve performance, which suggests identification is driven by a set of regular expressions matched against the input. The README does not say how it ranks or reports multiple matches.

brief.install_notes: No Homebrew-specific steps appear in the README. Options listed are: download a prebuilt executable from the GitHub releases page with no installation needed; cargo install lemmeknow; nix-env -iA nixpkgs.lemmeknow; or build from source with cargo (needs a Rust toolchain). For use as a library, add lemmeknow to Cargo.toml with version 0.7 and default-features = false, or point to the git repository. The crate supports wasm32-unknown-unknown. No accounts, hardware, or first-run configuration are mentioned.
brief.standout: Its speed claim is the headline: the README says it is about 33 times faster than PyWhat on an 8.7MB file and about 3 times faster on a single string, with benchmark charts. It also compiles to WebAssembly and has a browser front end, so the same identification logic can run in a web page.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a GitHub issues badge, stars and forks badges, and a Twitter link, but no release date, last commit date, or changelog. The README does reference version 0.7 for the crate. The scout note calls it a narrow tool; the README does not say it is abandoned or still active.
brief.caveats: The README gives no license text; it has only a GitHub license badge, so check the LICENSE file before reuse. The benchmarks are the author's and compare against PyWhat on a Windows executable (lemmeknow.exe vs pywhat floss.exe); treat the numbers as indicative. The tool is narrow: it identifies patterns in text, so it will not decode or crack arbitrary data, and the README does not list which formats it knows. Results depend on the regex set, which is community-maintained. The README contains no warnings about build difficulty.
quotes: The fastest way to identify anything
lemmeknow can be used for identifying mysterious text or to analyze hard-coded strings from captured network packets, malwares, or just about anything.
